Brodie
BROH-dee
noun (Gen-Z slang)
American: bro (clipped brother, a common American address since the mid-20th century) plus the affectionate diminutive ending -die, on the pattern of homie and buddy. Brodie spread through hip-hop and Black American speech in the 2010s and became everyday teen address by c. 2018–2020. A grandparent may know an unrelated older word: "to do a Brodie," a reckless leap or a spinning skid, from Steve Brodie, who claimed in 1886 to have jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang brodie is an affectionate "bro": your closest friend, the one you would vouch for — "that’s my brodie, he’s solid." The diminutive makes it warmer than plain bro; it is said with a hand on the shoulder. The Christian observation: the word reaches for something the Bible describes in its finest friendship passages. "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24). Solomon knew that a friend you choose can be truer than kin, and he praised the man who stays: "Thine own friend, and thy father’s friend, forsake not" (Pro 27:10). Friendship needs two because men fall: "if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecc 4:10). The Christian reads Proverbs 18:24 and sees Christ, the Friend who stuck closer than any brother when His own brothers did not yet believe Him, and who said to His disciples, "I have called you friends" (Joh 15:15). His friendship is measured in blood: "he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1Jn 3:16). A father tells his son: have a brodie, and be one — the friend who lifts him when he falls, tells him the truth, and would give up his own comfort, even his life, the way Christ gave His for you.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (American bro plus affectionate -die; hip-hop 2010s–present) for a close friend — a warm word the Bible fills with the friend that sticketh closer than a brother, Christ, who laid down His life for His friends.

expand to see more

BRODIE, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2015–present; hip-hop and Black American speech) A close friend; an affectionate "bro." "Me and brodie are going to the game."

Used as a name without an article ("brodie said…") or in address ("you good, brodie?"). Also spelled brody; broski is a cousin.

Unrelated older sense a grandparent may know: "to do a Brodie" — a reckless leap or a spinning car skid, after Steve Brodie’s claimed 1886 jump from the Brooklyn Bridge.

Webster (1828), root word brother: “BROTHER, noun plural brothers or brethren. [&hellip;] 1. A human male born of the same father and mother. A male by one of the parents only is called a half-brother, or brother of the half blood. 2. Any one closely united; an associate; as a band of brothers. 3. One that resembles another in manners.”

Decode for parents: clean and affectionate; it names your child’s closest friend, so learn who brodie is.

Key Scripture

Pro 18:24 — "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."

Pro 27:10 — "Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off."

Ecc 4:10 — "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

Joh 15:15 — "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you."

1Jn 3:16 — "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren."

Modern Corruption

Brodie is affectionate and clean; its only weakness is the friendship it often names — loyal to the crew, but not yet the friendship that lays down its life after the pattern of Christ.

expand to see more

Teenage boys need friends badly and rarely say so; brodie is one of the ways they say it. That is a good thing. Solomon wrote "woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecc 4:10), and a boy without a brodie is often a boy alone. The question a parent asks is not whether the word is acceptable but what the friendship is made of. Loyalty in the street sense — covering for each other, never telling, backing your boy whether he is right or wrong — is a counterfeit of the real thing.

Scripture shows the real thing. The friend that "sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24) is not the one who covers your sin, but the one who stays when you are low and speaks when you are wrong. Christ is that Friend perfectly. He calls His disciples "friends" (Joh 15:15) and then proves it with a cross, and John draws the line straight to us: "we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1Jn 3:16). Teach your son to be the kind of brodie who would give up his Saturday, his pride, or his reputation for a friend — because his Lord gave up far more.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English brothor → brother → American bro → bro plus diminutive -die → brodie in 2010s hip-hop → everyday teen address.

expand to see more

Old English brothor — brother

American bro — clipped address, common from the mid-20th century

Affectionate -ie / -die ending, as in homie, buddy, bestie

2010s hip-hop and Black American speech: brodie, a close friend

Unrelated: Steve Brodie (1886) and the phrase "to do a Brodie"

Usage

""Brodie stayed after practice to help me with my jump shot.""

"There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24) — be that friend."

"Christ laid down His life for us; we ought to lay down ours for the brethren (1Jn 3:16)."
